## TL;DR

CAPE-COD was a double blind, multi-center (conducted in France) placebo
controlled RCT of hydrocortisone in patients admitted to the ICU with severe
community acquired pneumonia (CAP). Death by day 28 was 6.2% with hydrocortisone
and 11.9% with placebo. The trial was stopped early at two thirds of its planned
size, on only 72 deaths. The effect size (a halving of mortality) is roughly
double what the trial was designed to detect, and is likely to be an
overestimate (see, "the winners curse"). It appears that this effect may have been
more pronounced in those with a higher CRP.
One of the main contrasting RCTs is
the REMAP-CAP corticosteroid domain, which has since stopped its fixed-course hydrocortisone arm for futility, with a point
estimate in the
direction of harm. REMAP-CAP steroid was open label, has a (very) small control arm, and 
so I do not believe it overturns CAPE-COD; it should, though, reduce our confidence in the application of these findings, and make us more open to new evidence as it emurges.

On the basis of the totality of the evidence, I would want to recieve
hydrocortisone for a severe bacterial pneumonia with a high inflammatory burden,
if I were a candidate for ICU.

## Background

The steroid evidence landscape in intensive care is complex. Really complex.
There are a number of conditions that may benefit from steroids including:
septic shock, meningitis and ARDS. The story in pneumonia is somewhat less
clear. A number of small RCTs---which were almost certainly underpowered---have
been unable to detect a mortality benefit, which should not be a surprise.

There are strong reasons of biological plausibility that severe bacterial
pneumonia would be susceptible to inflammatory modification with steroids.
However, there are rightly concerns about potential adverse sequelae of steroid
use: overly aggressive immune suppression, hyperglycaemia, improper timing (i.e.
initiating too soon or too late).

## Trial Overview

This trial was a double blind, placebo controlled, French multi-centre RCT
conducted at 31 centres from 2015 to 2020. Randomisation took place in a 1:1
fashion in blocks of four across strata (center and use of mechanical
ventilation). 1146 patients were needed to provide 80% power to detect a 25%
relative risk reduction in mortality from a baseline of 27%. This was increased
to 1165 to allow for two interim analyses, and rounded up to 1200 to account for
withdrawal of consent.

## PICO

- *Population:* adults admitted to the ICU with CAP, and at least one of four
severity criteria:
  - Mechanical ventilation (invasive or non-invasive) with PEEP
    of at least 5 cmH~2~O
  - High flow nasal oxygen with an FiO~2~ of at least 0.5 and a PaO~2~:FiO~2~ ratio below 40 kPa (300 mmHg)
  - A non-rebreathe mask with an estimated PaO~2~:FiO~2~ ratio below 40 kPa
  - A Pulmonary Severity Index above 130
  - *Key exclusions:* septic shock, a do-not-intubate order, influenza, suspected aspiration, long term steroid use and myelosuppression.
- *Intervention:* continuous infusion of hydrocortisone (200 mg / day) for 4 days,
started within 24 hours of meeting a severity criterion. At day 4, predefined
criteria for clinical improvement determined whether the patient received a
total course of 8 or 14 days, including a taper. Treatment stopped at ICU
discharge.
- *Comparator:* matched placebo (saline)
- *Outcomes:*
  - Primary: 28 day mortality.
  - Secondary: 90 day mortality, ICU length of stay, intubation or
non-invasive ventilation in those not ventilated at baseline, vasopressor
initiation, ventilator and vasopressor free days, change in PaO~2~:FiO~2~ ratio
and SOFA score by day 7, and SF-36 at day 90.
  - Safety: secondary infection, GI bleeding, daily insulin dose and weight gain.

Recruitment was paused at 800 randomised patients; the point of the planned
second interim analysis. This coincided with the COVID pandemic, and allowed
this group to pivot to investigating hydrocortisone in COVID-19, since the
research apparatus was already established. After a long (and very
understandable) pause, the DSMB recommended stopping the trial because:

1) Based on available data, equipoise no longer remained between groups.
2) long term suspension of the trial would have unknown impact on analysis
3) another 400 patients were very unlikely to change interpretation of results.

## In Context

| Study | Steroid | When? | Where? | Why? | How? | Who? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| 
| CAPE-COD | Hydrocortisone | Within 24 h of a severity criterion (median 15 h after ICU admission) | 31 ICUs, France | 28 day mortality | 200 mg/day infusion, then taper (8 or 14 days). Double blind | Severe CAP in ICU. No shock, no influenza. SAPS II 37, 22% intubated | 
| REMAP-CAP | Hydrocortisone | Within 24 h of ICU admission (median 8 h) | 101 sites, 18 countries | 90 day mortality | 50 mg QDS for 7 days, no taper. Open label | Severe CAP in ICU. Around half in shock, 7% influenza. APACHE II 18, 39% intubated |
| APROCCHSS | Hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone | Within 24 h of shock onset | France | 90 day mortality | 50 mg QDS plus 50 micrograms fludrocortisone for 7 days, no taper. Double blind | Septic shock (45% CAP). SAPS II 56, SOFA 11 to 12 |
| HYPRESS | Hydrocortisone | Within 48 h of organ dysfunction | 34 sites, Germany | Septic shock by day 14 | 200 mg/day infusion for 5 days, then taper. Double blind | Severe sepsis without shock |
| DEXA-ARDS | Dexamethasone | Within 30 h of ARDS onset | 17 ICUs, Spain | Ventilator free days | 20 mg daily for 5 days, then 10 mg daily for 5 days. Open label | Established moderate to severe ARDS |

## Results

5948 patients were assessed and 800 randomised; 795 were analysed. The single
largest reason for exclusion was septic shock (1200 patients). The median age
was 67 and 70% were male. At baseline, 22% were intubated, 22% were receiving
non-invasive ventilation, 42% high flow nasal oxygen and 14% a non-rebreathe
mask. The median SAPS II score was 37 to 38, the median SOFA score was 4, and
the median CRP was around 250 mg/L. Patients received the trial drug a median of
15 hours after ICU admission. No pathogen was isolated in 45% of patients.

The primary outcome, death from all causes by day 28, was 6.2% (25 of 400) in
the hydrocortisone arm and 11.9% (47 of 395) in the matched placebo arm. This
corresponds to a difference of -5.6% (-9.6% to -1.7%), p = 0.006 (chi square),
or a number needed to treat of 18. There are a number of secondary outcomes,
which I include graphically below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-secondary
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Secondary and safety outcomes from CAPE-COD, reported as hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals. A hazard ratio below 1 favours hydrocortisone. These intervals were not adjusted for multiplicity."

library(ggplot2)

secondary <- data.frame(
  outcome = c(
    "Intubation (no ventilation at baseline)",
    "Non-invasive ventilation (no ventilation at baseline)",
    "Intubation (not intubated at baseline)",
    "Vasopressor initiation (none at baseline)",
    "Hospital acquired infection",
    "GI bleeding" ),
  hr = c(0.59, 0.60, 0.69, 0.59, 0.87, 0.68),
  lo = c(0.40, 0.32, 0.50, 0.43, 0.57, 0.29),
  hi = c(0.86, 1.15, 0.94, 0.82, 1.34, 1.59) )

secondary$outcome <-
    factor(secondary$outcome, levels = rev(secondary$outcome))

ggplot(secondary, aes(x = hr, y = outcome)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") + 
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi)) +
  scale_x_log10() + 
  labs(x = "Hazard ratio (95% CI), hydrocortisone vs placebo", y = NULL) + 
  theme_minimal()
```

## Secondary Outcomes

The secondary outcomes were not adjusted for multiplicity, and the authors are
clear that they should be regarded as exploratory. I therefore describe
direction and size, and avoid the word "significant".

- No clear difference in:
  - Cumulative incidence of hospital acquired infection by day 28: 9.8 vs 11.1%
  - Cumulative incidence of GI bleeding by day 28: 2.2 vs 3.3%
  - Greater in intervention group 
  - Median daily dose of insulin by day 7, in those who received insulin: 35.5 vs 20.5 IU/day. More patients also needed insulin in the first place (231 vs 177). - Less in intervention group
  - Death by day 90: 9.3% vs 14.7%
  - Cumulative incidence of endotracheal intubation by day 28 in those not receiving any ventilation at baseline: 18.0 vs 29.5% -
Cumulative incidence of endotracheal intubation by day 28 in those not intubated
at baseline: 19.5% vs 27.7% - Cumulative incidence of vasopressor initiation by
day 28 in those not receiving at baseline: 15.3 vs 25.0%

These outcomes are coherent with the primary result. Fewer patients progressed
to intubation, fewer developed shock, and fewer died. This is the pattern we
would expect if steroids were interrupting the progression of the disease, and
it gives the mortality finding more credibility than it would have in isolation.

## Subgroups of Interest

The authors report that the effect on the primary outcome was consistent across
the subgroups examined: mechanical ventilation at baseline, age above or below
65, sex, a Pulmonary Severity Index above or below 130, a CRP above or below 150
mg/L, and whether a pathogen was isolated.

The subgroup I find most interesting is ventilation at baseline. Among patients
receiving mechanical ventilation at enrolment, mortality was 10.7% vs 14.3%.
Among those who were not, it was 2.7% vs 10.0%. This is a subgroup, and the
trial was not powered to detect an interaction. It is, though, at least
compatible with the idea that steroids are of most use early, before the patient
has declared themselves.

## Discussion

There are several important questions that arise from this trial. Rarely does a
trial give us everything we want and this one is no different.

### Were these patients sick?

The severity criteria were already quite lax in my view, and I can't explain the
rationale to change the eligibility criteria part way through the trial (the
PaO~2~:FiO~2~ threshold for patients on high flow nasal oxygen was relaxed from
200 to 300 mmHg). I'm not so sure if this truly is a trial of "severe"
pneumonia, but rather of pneumonia with an oxygen requirement. Perhaps they are
one and the same. Further, these were not very sick patients. A median SAPS II
of 37 and a median SOFA of 4 demonstrate this, as does the fact that fewer than
a quarter were intubated. Contrast this with APROCCHSS, where the mean SAPS II
was 56. The enrolment criteria were never going to produce a mortality of 27%
and indeed, a much lower control group mortality (11.9%) is exactly what we saw.

<!-- TODO (Ed): the detail of the eligibility amendment (200 to 300 mmHg, spring
2017, after 285 patients) is from Wiki Journal Club, not the protocol. Please
check. -->

It is of interest to highlight that although septic shock was an exclusion
criterion, 10 to 13% of patients were receiving a vasopressor at baseline. Shock
is a spectrum, and this trial sits at the mild end of it.

### How much should we trust the size of the effect?

This is the part of the trial I am least comfortable with. The trial was
designed to detect a 25% relative risk reduction. It observed one of 47%. Either
hydrocortisone is twice as effective as its own investigators hoped, or the
estimate is inflated. I think the latter is more likely, for three reasons.

First, the trial stopped at two thirds of its planned size. Trials that stop
early with a favourable result overestimate the treatment effect on average;
this is a well described phenomenon. The decision to stop was also not a clean
one. The interim result (p = 0.006) is nowhere near the very stringent threshold
that Peto's rule sets for an interim analysis, and so the trial was not stopped
for crossing a boundary. It was stopped because of a mixture of an encouraging
result and the practical difficulty of restarting after the pandemic. I have
sympathy for the DSMB, though I find it difficult to reconcile "equipoise no
longer remained" with a result that did not meet the trial's own stopping rule.

Second, the baseline mortality was less than half that anticipated. The trial was
arguably therefore substantially *underpowered* to detect a plausible effect, and an underpowered
trial that reaches significance does so by overestimating.

None of this invalidates the findings. But it does suggest caution that the likely
effect size is going to be far smaller in practice than the one we have observed.

### Translating to the UK

All these patients were inside the ICU. It's hard to translate this directly
into the UK, which is seemingly more resource restricted, by comparison. Many of
the patients in this trial would be managed on the ward in a UK environment. And
so this raises the question, should we start steroids outside the ICU in those
eligible?

Although I view the point of admission to the ICU as a largely administrative
time point, it does create a different safety profile for the patient, some
positive, some negative. For those who think admission to the ICU is a slam dunk
positive intervention, I would invite them to read the ICE-CUB 2 trial, in which
a programme of systematic ICU admission for critically ill elderly patients did
not reduce 6 month mortality. Inside the ICU I can site an art line, closely
monitor both haemodynamics and gas exchange, and trivially run a variable rate
insulin infusion to control hyperglycaemia. This may offer a favourable safety
advantage in this context that I can't replicate on the ward.

An infusion of steroid is
less realistically achievable in a UK ward setting. I think a pragmatic use of
QDS hydrocortisone is reasonable; it can be administered on ward rounds, and won't occupy another line when central access isn't going to be availible. This requires buy in from parent teams who
will be looking after the patients outside ICU and will have to contend with the
inevitable hyperglycaemia. Though we do have large scale institutional memory of this
from COVID.

Does this finding translate to patients who are not candidates for ICU? I would
say no. This is a fundamentally different patient population. Typically much
more frail, and susceptible to the adverse sequelae of steroids, particularly
outside the ICU. The trial excluded patients with a do-not-intubate order (212
of those screened), and it did not measure the harms I would be most concerned
about in this group; delirium and neuromuscular weakness were not assessed, and
the reversibility of the hyperglycaemia was not examined. I don't think you can
extrapolate that far from this trial. There will be a strong cross contaminating
"action" bias from this study (i.e. there will be cultural awareness that steroids
are used in severe CAP, and so we must do "everything" we can for ward level patients)
which I would strongly caution against. This trial doesn't opine on that group,
and I could easily create a physiological argument for both harm and help in this group;
equipoise remains.

### Was this bacterial pneumonia?

Mostly. Microbiological
testing was left to the treating team. Influenza testing was recommended during
epidemic periods and was not mandated. No pathogen was found in 45% of patients.
I think it is fair to say that this was a trial of presumed bacterial pneumonia
in which a reasonable attempt to exclude influenza was undertaken.
In my institute, my feeling is that we probably test for more viral respiratory
pathogens, which is a practice that has in a small part come out of the pandemic.
I think this is an important nuance of the trial, as a negative
respiratory viral PCR should be part of the decision to treat, doubly so in
seasonal periods.

## Putting CAPE-COD in Context

There are many steroid trials in intensive care, though four major trials
come to mind that may contribute to interpretation here.

### DEXA-ARDS

First, DEXA-ARDS, which has several notable flaws. Most strikingly, the lack of
appropriate blinding and the lack of any meaningful excess of
hyperglycaemia in the treatment arm (76% vs 70%) which has always bothered me.
It was also stopped early, for
slow recruitment. While I cannot ignore the findings, and I
would probably administer dexamethasone to patients with established ARDS, I
would want another trial to be conducted that essentially bridges these two
trials. A properly blinded ARDS trial, where prior steroid use wasn't an
exclusion criterion. The question would then be, does a patient who has already
received hydrocortisone for their pneumonia, and who progresses to ARDS
regardless, benefit from escalation to dexamethasone?

At present we would be implementing findings by moving from one trial population
to another, and I don't think we can say with any degree of certainty what 
the effect of steroids would be in that context.

### APROCCHSS

Second, APROCCHSS, which was a double blind randomised controlled trial
investigating the use of hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone in established
septic shock. I'll make a timely joke that if you want a steroid trial to 
be positive in ICM, then make sure Anand conducts it.
Briefly, patients in this trial were much sicker, with a minimum
noradrenaline requirement of 0.25 micrograms/kg/min (This is a heck of a lot
of noradrenaline), commensurate SAPS II and
SOFA scores, and a control group mortality of 49.1% at 90 days (vs 43.0% with
treatment). These were very sick patients.
Although this was all comers with sepsis, the single largest group
was severe community acquired pneumonia. A subsequent subgroup analysis of the
562 patients with CAP found 90 day mortality of 39% with treatment and 51% with
placebo (OR 0.60, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.83), with no apparent effect in the 648
patients without CAP (OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.29). Again, this study excluded
those who were exposed to prior steroids.

<!-- TODO (Ed): I could not find the 0.25 micrograms/kg/min threshold in the
sources I was able to open; it is your figure and matches my recollection of the
paper. Worth a quick check. -->

There is now an abundance of data to show that steroids in septic shock speed
shock resolution, and likely improve mortality. CAPE-COD and APROCCHSS are
complementary; one excluded shock and the other required it, and both point in
the same direction for pneumonia.

### HYPRESS

Third, HYPRESS, which used steroids (hydrocortisone only) in sepsis in an
attempt to *prevent* the onset of shock. It did not. Septic shock developed in
21.2% of the hydrocortisone group and 22.9% of the placebo group, and there was
no difference in mortality.

This is harder to square away with CAPE-COD, in which
hydrocortisone appeared to prevent vasopressor initiation (15.3% vs 25.0%) using
a very similar regimen. This could be used as an argument to add weight to the evidence that CAPE-COD
may be a victim of the winners curse. The counter argument, and the one I prefer, is that HYPRESS is a victim
of the heterogenity of sepsis, and by CAPE-COD narrowing down on a more specific 
disease entity (that of primarily bacterial pneumonia) then a biological signal
may be more apparent. This is a complex discussion for another day.

### REMAP-CAP

Last, and the most directly comparable, is the REMAP-CAP corticosteroid domain.

REMAP-CAP is an international, open label, adaptive platform trial. Patients
admitted to the ICU with severe CAP, requiring respiratory or cardiovascular
organ support, were randomised to hydrocortisone 50 mg every 6 hours for 7 days,
or to no steroid. The arm was stopped for futility; there was less than a 5%
probability that hydrocortisone reduced the odds of death by more than 20%. 90
day mortality was 15% (78 of 521) with hydrocortisone and 9.8% (12 of 122) with
control. The pooled adjusted odds ratio was 1.56 (95% credible interval 0.80 to
3.31), with a 90% posterior probability of harm.

These two trials are not easily reconciled. The unadjusted odds ratio for death
in CAPE-COD is 0.49 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.82, my calculation). The intervals barely
touch. So what is going on? I can see several candidate explanations, and I do
not think any of them is sufficient alone.

**REMAP-CAP is imprecise.** The control arm contained 122 patients and 12
deaths. The entire comparison hinges on those 12 events. A control group
mortality of 9.8% is also surprisingly low for a population in which nearly half
were in shock and 38% were intubated; it is lower than the placebo arm of
CAPE-COD (14.7% at day 90), which excluded shock. I don't entirely know what
went on here, but I wonder if this is an incredbly noisy sample (being so small)
which has captured a control arm that was doing much better by chance, than 
severity should have suggested.

**The arms were not well balanced.** Patients assigned to hydrocortisone were older (62.5
vs 58.5 years), more hypoxaemic and had more cardiovascular dysfunction. A third
of them were enrolled at sites that would not randomise to control, because
those clinicians lacked equipoise (i.e. they wanted to give steroids). 
A data labelling error also
distorted the response adaptive randomisation. The model adjusts for site and
severity, and the result held when restricted to sites offering both arms.
Adjustment in a sample this small can only do so much.

**It was open label.**
23% of control patients received a steroid, although usually a short course.
This would dilute a benefit. It would not manufacture a signal of harm.

**The population differed.** REMAP-CAP included shock and influenza; CAPE-COD excluded
both. This does not rescue the situation. The APROCCHSS subgroup suggests that
pneumonia with shock is where steroids work best, and yet the estimate in the
REMAP-CAP shock stratum (OR 1.53) was no better than elsewhere.

**The regimen differed.** CAPE-COD used an infusion with a response guided taper. REMAP-CAP
used intermittent boluses and stopped abruptly at day 7. The survival curves in
REMAP-CAP overlap for the first fortnight and separate thereafter, which is at
least compatible with a rebound in inflammation after abrupt cessation. This is
speculation on my part. It is weakened by the fact that APROCCHSS used the same
bolus regimen without a taper and was positive.

**Timing does not explain it.** The CAPE-COD authors propose that early treatment may account for their
result. Patients in REMAP-CAP were treated a median of 8 hours after ICU
admission, which is earlier than in CAPE-COD.

**Inflammation may matter more than severity.** The median CRP in CAPE-COD was around 250 mg/L. An individual patient data meta-analysis of eight trials (Smit and colleagues, 2025) found
that the benefit of steroids in CAP was concentrated in patients with a CRP
above 204 mg/L. REMAP-CAP does not report CRP. It is possible that the two
trials enrolled patients with a similar need for organ support and quite
different inflammatory phenotypes. This would be my leading hypothesis, though
it remains a hypothesis.

It is also worth saying that the positive results in this area (CAPE-COD, and
APROCCHSS with its CAP subgroup) all come from one country and overlapping
networks of investigators. I do not suggest anything improper. Replication
outside the system that generated a finding is how we learn whether it travels,
and REMAP-CAP is the first serious attempt at that.

There was one point of agreement. In REMAP-CAP the duration of cardiovascular
support was shorter with hydrocortisone (median 2 vs 3 days). Faster shock
resolution is the most reproducible effect of steroids in critical illness, and
it appears here too.

Where does this leave us? REMAP-CAP tells us that a very large benefit from a
fixed 7 day course of hydrocortisone, applied to all comers with severe CAP in
ICU, is unlikely. 
CAPE-COD tells us that there may be a benefit in a more selected group. Taken
together, I think the most credible explanasion is that there is a modest benefit,
probably smaller than CAPE-COD reported, and probably not uniform across
all patients.

### Caution: Interaction with DNAR orders

Both trials enrolled patients who were for full escalation. CAPE-COD excluded
those with a do-not-intubate order. REMAP-CAP excluded nursing home residents
and those for whom there was no commitment to full support. Neither can tell us
anything about the patient with a ward based ceiling of care, who makes up a
large share of pneumonia deaths in the UK.

## The Friends and Family Test

My "acid" test for interpreting trial literature is whether or not you would want
the treatment for yourself or family members. I find it's a helpful heuristic to
follow and challenges us to bridge the gap between our intellectual side
(interpreting trial evidence in the cold) and our emotional side (where the
stakes are very high). I have, on occasion, also found myself committing to doing 
something in an academic context, and then feeling far more nervous about it
when its actually my decision at the bedside, and the stakes are high.
This is my way of trying to wrestle with this now, in a more public way, so
that I'm not spending my decision making budget during a critical period.

If I (or a close family member) had a bacterial pneumonia, with an oxygen requirement, would I want to receive steroids? Yes. With a few qualifiers.

Taken in the context above, I think any potentia harms of steroids have been fairly
well identified and are both modest and manageable;
contrasting with the potential benefit for increased survival.
If my CRP were high (above 200) and my flu swab negative, I would not hesitate.
If my flu swab was positive, I'd want to be enrolled in a trial (like RECOVERY) because I
want randomised care, not random care.
If I had an oxygen requirement, but my CRP was much lower, say under 100, I would be much less certain. I think I'd probably still want them, but honestly, I don't think I'd mind
too much either way.

And so my practice will continue to promote the use of steroids in bacterial pneumonia
with an oxygen requirement in patients eligible for admission to the ICU, particularly
in those with a high inflammatory phenome, as characterised by their CRP.

## Wrapping Up

CAPE-COD showed that hydrocortisone improved mortality in a population of
patients with presumed bacterial pneumonia, who were being treated inside an
ICU, with an oxygen requirement, who were not in shock, and in whom influenza
had not been identified. The effect was probably overestimated, and REMAP-CAP (a subsequent
open label platform trial) was unable to reproduce its findings.

I think equipoise remains in two places. First, in the frail or elderly
population who are ineligible for treatment inside the ICU. Second, in those with
reletively low CRPs, in whom significant inflamation is thought not to be an issue.
I would randomise between steroids and placebo in patients that meet the standard CAPE-COD
crtieria, but have a very low inflammatory phenome. Last, those that go on to develop
ARDS physiology but who were already started on steroids. I don't know what to do
with these patients, are prior RCTs have generally excluded them ("prior steroid exposure").

## My Recommendations

- Hydrocortisone should be considered for patients with "severe" CAP, who:
  - meet inclusion criteria listed above (pragmatically, I would use CURB-65 instead of the PSI. Since thats already baked into standard UK practice.)
  - are being *considered* for admission to the ICU (so we can start steroids early,
prior to admission to the ICU, and continue in line with the CAPE-COD protocol)
  - where influenza has been tested and excluded.
- with greater confidence where the CRP is high (above approximately 200 mg/L)
- Pragmatically, consider dosing at 50 mg QDS, and implement the taper used in the trial (or stop at ICU discharge)
- Add in fludrocortisone if the patient develops septic shock.
- Switch to high dose dexamethasone if the patient develops severe ARDS.

- Consider a more liberal use of procalcitonin in these patients, since we would
lose the signal from white cells (and to a lesser extent CRP) to monitor for secondary infective
complications.
